solutions.check: 31 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Infuriated police captain casually dumping Ian

indicators.note: Doing a thing casually is doing it without care for the proper order, so the letters beside the word come out however they fall.
To dump something is to get rid of it, so the name that follows leaves the pile before anything is rearranged.

parts.note: thirteen letters to work from, three more than the grid has room for
the three letters that go, wherever they sit among the thirteen

explanation.surface: A senior officer dropping a colleague without ceremony, and raging while he does it.
explanation.walkthrough: Thirteen letters are offered for a ten-letter entry, and that count is the tell that something has to come out before anything is rearranged. Ian reads as a man being let go rather than as three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone apoplectic is angry to the point of looking fit to burst a blood vessel, which is what infuriated describes at its strongest.

clue.text: Very old Cyclops had to defecate

parts.note: v is the standing short form of very
o is the crossword's letter for old
the setter writing about himself says I had, contracted to I'd

explanation.surface: A one-eyed giant of great age with an urgent need.
explanation.walkthrough: Cyclops is the setter's own pen name, so the first person in the wordplay is him and 'Cyclops had' shortens to I'd. The definition is the clinical verb a doctor uses for emptying the bowels, the one polite word in the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: To void is the medical verb for emptying the bowels or the bladder, so it stands in for defecate without the vulgarity.

clue.text: US state's appropriate bigmouth

parts.note: GA is the two-letter postal code for Georgia
the contracted 's joins on as a letter of its own
to bag a thing is to appropriate it, to take it for yourself

explanation.surface: The loudmouth a particular American state deserves.
explanation.walkthrough: Appropriate reads as the adjective, fitting or suitable, and is the verb to grab. The apostrophe-s looks like plain possession and is quietly a letter of the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A gasbag is someone who talks and talks without saying much, which is what calling a person a bigmouth means.

clue.text: Dismiss going on stage, screwing Reg — that's criminal

indicators.note: In a down entry what goes on something is written above it, so the first piece sits on top of the second.
To screw a thing is to twist it round, so the name beside the word does not stay in the order it is printed.

parts.note: to boot somebody out is to dismiss them
a leg of a race or a tour is one stage of it
the three letters of the name, re-set

explanation.surface: A man sacked as he steps on stage for what he has been doing to Reg.
explanation.walkthrough: Screwing is the Eye's word for sex on the surface and a plain twist in the wordplay, which is why only three letters move. Stage is the leg of a journey rather than the boards.
explanation.definitionFit: A bootlegger deals in liquor or recordings made and sold illegally, so criminal names the trade rather than describing the man.

clue.text: Peel's people

parts.note: the contracted 's, standing on its own as a letter
your kin are your people, the relatives you belong to

explanation.surface: The men Sir Robert Peel gave Britain its police force with.
explanation.walkthrough: Peel reads as Sir Robert Peel, who founded the Metropolitan Police in 1829 and whose constables were nicknamed peelers; in the wordplay it is the rind on an orange. Two words of clue leave nowhere for an indicator to hide.
explanation.definitionFit: The peel of an orange or a potato is its skin, the same outer layer under either name.

clue.text: What dozy type wants: to close magazine

parts.note: to close a door is to shut it
the Eye is Private Eye, the magazine this crossword is printed in

explanation.surface: A sleepy sort who only wants the magazine shut so he can drop off.
explanation.walkthrough: The magazine is the one in your hands: Cyclops sets for Private Eye and has put its name in its own grid. The colon does the joining and instructs nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Shut-eye is the informal word for sleep, which is precisely what a dozy person is after.

clue.text: Negotiator told a PM to "shift and get one in!"

indicators.note: To shift things is to move them out of where they were, so the letters named do not stay in their printed order.

parts.note: seven letters to be re-set
one is the Roman numeral I, and getting it in adds it to the letters being shifted

explanation.surface: Somebody shouting at a prime minister to get out of the way and buy a round.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is a shout across a bar, and 'shift' there is British for move yourself rather than rearrange. Getting one in is standing a round, which is how an eighth letter arrives unnoticed.
explanation.definitionFit: A diplomat's job is negotiating between governments, so negotiator names the work rather than the office.

clue.text: Luxury yacht assistant's reported period?

indicators.note: Something reported is passed on by mouth, so what matters about the words in front is the noise they make, not their spelling.

parts.note: an aide is an assistant and the working surface of a yacht is its deck, so the helper up there is a deck aide

explanation.surface: A rich man's boat and the stint his personal assistant is said to work.
explanation.walkthrough: Period wants to be a full stop or a woman's cycle and is a stretch of years. The question mark is honest about the sound: deck aide is not a job title anyone prints, only two ordinary words run together.
explanation.definitionFit: A decade is ten years, one of the stock lengths of time that English calls a period.

clue.text: Pirate captain with a hard on — puffy thing

definitions.note: Puffy here means to do with puffing rather than swollen, so the phrase describes the object by the action it exists for instead of naming it.

indicators.note: In an across entry what is written on something has been reached after it, so the letters in front of the word go behind the captain.

parts.note: Captain Hook is the pirate in Peter Pan, named for the iron hand
the article, taken as it stands
H is the grade stamped on a hard pencil

explanation.surface: A pirate captain with an erection, called something that puffs.
explanation.walkthrough: A hard-on is the joke the sentence is built round, and those two words come apart into an article and a pencil grade. Hook is a named character, not the implement.
explanation.definitionFit: A hookah is the water pipe that smokers draw tobacco smoke through, so puffy names it by the puffing it is built for.

clue.text: Archer going by a different name in Piccadilly

definitions.meaning: read as a bowman, and meant as the Roman god of love, who is drawn with a bow and a quiver

definitions.text: going by a different name in Piccadilly
definitions.meaning: the winged figure on the fountain in Piccadilly Circus has been called Eros for over a century, and Eros is the Greek name for the same god

explanation.surface: A man with a bow living in central London under an alias.
explanation.walkthrough: The statue at Piccadilly Circus is known to every Londoner as Eros, and Eros is Greek; the grid wants the Roman name for the same god. No part of the sentence hands over letters, so it has to be read twice instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Cupid is the Roman god of love, always shown with a bow, and the Piccadilly Circus statue of him is universally called Eros, his Greek name.

clue.text: Plague caused by drug in the cream

indicators.note: What is in a thing sits inside it, so the letter before the word goes between the letters after it.

parts.note: the cream of anything is the best of it, the pick of the crop; the word parts after its first letter
E is the tablet, ecstasy

explanation.surface: An outbreak blamed on something slipped into the finest of the batch.
explanation.walkthrough: Cream is the pick of a group rather than anything in a jug. Plague is the verb and not the disease, which is what lets five letters stand in for it.
explanation.definitionFit: To beset someone is to hound them from every side, which is what plague means as a verb — troubles, doubts and reporters all do it.

clue.text: Like judges' robes, pants?

indicators.note: Pants is British slang for rubbish, and letters called rubbish are not to be trusted to stay in the order they were printed.

parts.note: the five letters of the garment, to be re-set

explanation.surface: A rude verdict on what the bench wears to court.
explanation.walkthrough: Sober as a judge is the idiom the definition leans on, and it is about the men and women, not the wardrobe. Pants is the playground word for rubbish, which is what lets it shake the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom sober as a judge makes the bench the standard for gravity and abstinence, so being like judges is being sober.

clue.text: (& 24dn.) Nick Love would be scrapped by Reform UK

definitions.text: would be scrapped by Reform UK
definitions.note: The entry is named by the policy one party has promised to abolish rather than by a synonym, so a whole clause stands where a noun phrase would.

parts.note: to nick a thief is to catch him, as a fisherman catches fish with a mesh
love is the tennis scoreboard's nothing

explanation.surface: A man called Nick Love whose post Reform UK would abolish.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick Love is a real British film director, which is why the two capitals sit together so innocently. Reform UK campaigns on scrapping the 2050 emissions target, and that target runs three letters here and four at 24 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Net zero is the pledge to balance greenhouse gases emitted against gases taken back out of the air, and tearing it up has been a standing Reform UK manifesto line.

clue.text: Experiencing a fast, contrived edit in Guardian leader

indicators.note: Something contrived has been worked up out of its parts rather than found, so the letters beside the word are re-set.

parts.note: the six letters of those two words, re-set

indicators.note: The leader of a word is the letter at its head, so only the first letter of the newspaper's name is taken.

parts.note: the newspaper's initial

explanation.surface: A hungry sub-editor working a contrived change into a Guardian editorial.
explanation.walkthrough: A leader in a British paper is the editorial, which is why 'Guardian leader' reads as one thing and works as two. The comma after fast is the only sign the definition has ended.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone dieting is deliberately going without food, which is what experiencing a fast describes, and both wear the -ing.

clue.text: Screwing quietly, in a state of imbalance

indicators.note: To screw something up is to crumple it, and letters crumpled together come out in a different order.

parts.note: ten letters to be re-set, the comma no obstacle

explanation.surface: Furtive sex in a country that has lost its balance.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is only the last three words, so 'in a' has to be pulled back off it and thrown into the mixture — the commonest trap a long anagram sets. Quietly goes in whole, not as the musician's p.
explanation.definitionFit: Inequality is the condition of some having far more than others, which is a state of imbalance in the plainest sense.

clue.text: Incapable? Don't get involved in a piss-up here, then

definitions.meaning: read as a warning to somebody who cannot hold their drink, and meant as the verdict the idiom below passes on hopeless organisers

definitions.text: Don't get involved in a piss-up here, then
definitions.meaning: British English measures total incompetence by saying a person could not organise a piss-up in the one building already awash with beer, and 'here' points at that building

explanation.surface: Advice to a lightweight drinker: stay away from this particular party.
explanation.walkthrough: Couldn't organise a piss-up in a brewery is the standard British verdict on hopeless management, and the clue runs it backwards, naming the place and leaving the insult implied. There are no letters to find anywhere in the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A brewery is where beer is made by the tankful, which is why the idiom picks it as the easiest imaginable venue for a drinking session.

clue.text: Article stuck in injured testes (endlessly on the job), incurring one-time tax

indicators.note: To stick a thing in is to push it inside, so the article lands between the letters that come out of the shuffle.
Something done endlessly has no end, so the word loses its final letter before anything else happens.
An injured body does not hold its shape, so the word beside the term comes apart and its letters are re-set.

parts.note: the word docked of its last letter and the five that remain re-set, parting to take what goes inside
the indefinite article, taken as it stands
a worker on the job is on duty

explanation.surface: Damaged testicles that never get a day off, and a tax bill on top of it.
explanation.walkthrough: One-time means former, not one-off: Britain charged estate duty on what the dead left behind until 1975, when capital transfer tax took over. Article is the grammarian's a, not a piece of writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Estate duty was the tax the state took out of a dead person's property, and Britain stopped levying it in 1975, so one-time means former rather than single.

clue.text: Farage claims it's not Reform's position to get pissed about her RAF movement

definitions.text: Farage claims it's not Reform's position
definitions.note: The entry is named by the label a party leader keeps rejecting rather than by a synonym, so a reported denial stands where a noun phrase would.

indicators.note: What goes about a thing wraps round it, so the word for drunk splits and the letters named next sit in the gap.
A movement is things shifting out of place, so the two words beside it are set down in another order.

parts.note: tight is one of British English's many words for drunk; it parts after its first letter
the six letters of those two words, re-set

explanation.surface: Nigel Farage rejecting a label, and a reason to get drunk over her air-force posting.
explanation.walkthrough: Movement reads as a political movement — exactly the sort the definition is about — and is the shuffle instruction. Reform UK has spent its short life denying the label the answer gives it.
explanation.definitionFit: The far right is the political ground ultra-nationalist parties stand on, and Nigel Farage insists at every opportunity that Reform UK does not stand there.

clue.text: Broadcast reform over which blood was spilt?

definitions.note: The place is described by what happened at it rather than named, so a relative clause stands where a noun would; the question mark marks the stretch.

indicators.note: To broadcast is to put a thing out over the air, so the word that follows is wanted as a sound rather than as a spelling.

parts.note: to reform a thing is to alter it, and said aloud that word gives no hint which of its two spellings is meant

explanation.surface: A change to the law announced after bloodshed.
explanation.walkthrough: Reform is the word this puzzle keeps returning to — the party turns up at 12 across and 17 across — and here it is the plain verb. Sacrificial blood on stone is the older picture the question mark asks you to accept.
explanation.definitionFit: An altar is the stone where sacrifices were killed and offered up, so blood spilt across it is the oldest thing about it.

clue.text: Liberal in favour of something that might be blown

parts.note: pro is the Latin for in favour of, as in pro-European
a fuse blows when the current running through it is too strong

explanation.surface: A Liberal backing a scheme that could go up in smoke.
explanation.walkthrough: Liberal reads as the party member and is the adjective meaning generous. Blown does the pointing: what blows in a fusebox is a strip of wire, and the capital L is there to keep you looking at Westminster.
explanation.definitionFit: Profuse apologies and profuse bleeding both come in unstinting quantity, which is liberal in the generous sense rather than the political one.

clue.text: Exhibitionist broadcaster consuming heroin

indicators.note: To consume something is to take it in, so the drug's letter is swallowed by the letters either side of it.

parts.note: to broadcast seed is to fling it wide across a field by hand, which is what a sower does; the word parts after its first letter
H is the street letter for heroin

explanation.surface: A television presenter with a drug habit and a taste for attention.
explanation.walkthrough: Broadcasting was a farming word for centuries before it was a radio one, and the farming sense is the one wanted. Exhibitionist is the definition and the only word in the clue not about media or drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: A shower is one who shows, so an exhibitionist — somebody who cannot resist displaying themselves — is a shower in the plainest formation of the word.

clue.text: To do with matter demanded by narrowly-losing candidate?

definitions.note: The entry is named by who calls for it rather than by a synonym, so a participle phrase stands where a noun would; the question mark marks the stretch.

parts.note: re is the heading on a memo, meaning about or concerning
what counts is what matters, both words carrying the sense of weighing

explanation.surface: A candidate beaten by a handful of votes making a demand about the matter.
explanation.walkthrough: The two halves join with no link word at all, which is why 'to do with matter' reads as one idea and works as two. Counting is the joke underneath: the answer is itself a second count.
explanation.definitionFit: A recount is the second count of ballots a beaten candidate can call for when the margin is thin, so the clue names it by what produces it.

clue.text: Warm-up exercise's second time — vomit

parts.note: s is the clock's short form for second
t is the physicist's letter for time
to retch is to heave as though about to be sick

explanation.surface: An athlete timing a warm-up and being sick on the second go.
explanation.walkthrough: Second and time sit side by side so naturally that they read as one phrase, and each is a separate single letter. The dash is punctuation and instructs nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A stretch is the pull an athlete puts through a muscle before exercise, which is the commonest warm-up exercise there is.

clue.text: Todger just begun to be inserted in excited, messy way

indicators.note: A thing just begun has got no further than its start, so only the first letter of the word is taken.
Somebody excited will not keep still, and letters told they are excited do not keep their printed order.

parts.note: the five letters of the word re-set, parting to take what goes inside

indicators.note: To insert is to push inside, so that letter goes between the letters of what follows.

parts.note: the first letter of the word, taken on its own

explanation.surface: A penis barely in, and the excitable mess it is making.
explanation.walkthrough: Todger is British slang for a penis, which is the whole of the surface and contributes exactly one letter. Way is the definition, the shortest word in the clue and the easiest to walk past.
explanation.definitionFit: A system is a settled way of doing something — a filing system, a betting system — so way covers it exactly.

clue.text: Iron character, ultimately it goes to one's head

definitions.note: The thing is defined by where it is worn rather than named, so a whole clause stands in for a noun and borrows the idiom about success.

indicators.note: Ultimately means at the very end, so what is wanted is the last of the things named rather than any of the rest.

parts.note: Fe is iron's symbol on the periodic table, from the Latin ferrum
the characters of the alphabet run to twenty-six, and the last of them is the one wanted

explanation.surface: A person of iron will whose success has gone to their head.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the sentence are figures of speech — an iron character, something going to your head — and both are dead literal in the wordplay. The answer is the tasselled red hat of Morocco and the old Ottoman empire.
explanation.definitionFit: A fez is the brimless felt hat worn across North Africa and the old Ottoman world, so it goes on a head and nowhere else.

clue.text: see 12ac.
Legislative body that's no stranger to spin

definitions.note: The second half points at a cricket ground by what happens on its pitch rather than naming it, so a description stands where a synonym would.
definitions.meaning: the upper of Parliament's two chambers, whose members sit by title rather than by election
the cricket ground in St John's Wood that the English game treats as its home, where spin bowling turns up in every match played

explanation.surface: The upper house of Parliament, thoroughly used to having its message managed.
explanation.walkthrough: Spin is the political sort in the sentence and the bowler's sort in the second definition. The cricket ground takes an apostrophe on its scoreboard and the grid quietly drops it.
explanation.definitionFit: The House of Lords is Parliament's upper chamber, and Lord's is the ground where spinners have been turning the ball since the game was first written down.

clue.text: Whose partner departed one day in shock

definitions.note: The person is described by what has happened to her rather than named, so a relative clause stands where a noun would.

indicators.note: What goes in a thing is put inside it, so the two letters before the word are set between the letters after it.

parts.note: to wow an audience is to knock them sideways, which is to shock them; the word parts after its first letter
the Roman numeral one
d is the diary's short form for day

explanation.surface: Somebody whose other half walked out one shocking day.
explanation.walkthrough: Departed reads as walked out and means died, and that single word carries the whole misdirection. Shock is a verb here, the thing a stage act does to a crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: A widow is a woman whose husband or partner has died, and departed is the undertaker's own word for exactly that.

clue.text: Republican in latest upset, a chirpy individual

indicators.note: What is in a thing sits inside it, so the letter before the word goes between the letters after it.
In a down entry the letters climb from the bottom of the column, so the word named is written the other way about.

parts.note: the latest thing is the new one; those three letters are then read backwards and part to take what goes inside
R is the letter printed beside a Republican's name on an American ballot

explanation.surface: A Republican caught up in the most recent scandal, and a cheerful soul with it.
explanation.walkthrough: Upset reads as the political shock in the sentence and as a turning-round instruction in the wordplay, the one word doing both jobs. Chirpy is meant literally: the bird's song is far louder than the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A wren is the tiny brown garden bird whose song is startlingly loud for its size, so a chirpy individual names it by the noise it makes.

clue.text: Guarantee to stick old rock star in the pen

indicators.note: To stick something somewhere is to shove it in without ceremony, which is the instruction to bury one piece in another.
In says where it goes: between the letters of the word that follows.

parts.note: a sty is the pen a pig is kept in; the word parts after its first letter
the surname of Midge Ure, who fronted Ultravox in the early 1980s

explanation.surface: Promising to shove an ageing rocker into a pigsty.
explanation.walkthrough: Pen is the pigsty, not the writing implement or the American prison, both of which the sentence would happily take. Ure also wrote Do They Know It's Christmas? with Bob Geldof, which is what keeps him famous enough to clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A surety is the money or the person standing behind a promise, which is what a guarantee is in both the legal and the everyday sense.

clue.text: Force Ted out (backslider)

indicators.note: Something out of true is out of its proper order, so the two words in front are set down in another arrangement.

parts.note: eight letters to be re-set

explanation.surface: Throwing a man called Ted off the squad.
explanation.walkthrough: Force out is a single phrasal verb on the surface and the clue splits it: force belongs to the letters, out is the instruction. The definition sits alone in brackets, which is unusual enough to be a signpost.
explanation.definitionFit: A defector abandons the side he belonged to for the other one, and backslider is the older word for anybody who falls away from an allegiance or a faith.
